questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The city, the culture, having the possibility to speak English and have English-spoken classes as well as the university not being considered academically bad.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
In general, I had a really good experience with my exchange. I liked my classes, the level of teaching and workload was similar to KU. I felt that the university and teachers were very helpful if I had any issues. 
I had a few issues with the place I was staying at, but it got solved.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: VU was good at sending out information (emails) and they were good at helping one upon arrival. There were also always people at the university ready to help you with any questions including directions around campus.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: See comment above

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Some things could have been done a bit better on the introduction day, but they were all very helpful

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I paid a fee (205 euros) to the university so that I could book accommodation through their online platform. The booking itself was a nightmare as the platform opened up at a certain date and time meaning that the platform was very slow and overwhelmed with too many people logging on at the same time. I still managed to get something though very expensive (but everything is when it comes to accommodation, only the student housings on campus are fairly cheap). Although it is a big fee, it really was helpful as there is a lack of accommodations. I think I would have had difficulties finding housing for myself if I had to do it by myself.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There will be parties and other activities happening at the student housing on campus, which will be more difficult to attend since you'll live further away. However, I found it to be okay, as I easily could come to campus or the area with student housing (which is not ON campus, but close to it. It doesn't take that long to walk/bike or take the tram). Where I lived (the Social Hub West) I could get to campus and the city center in about 20-30 min by bike or public transport, which suited me very well. I had a metro and tram station right next to my accommodation, but I know that some had about a km or more to a metro station.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There was a good selection. However, there is a shortening of housing. So be prepared to spend some time on it, because it might be difficult to get something. That said, it shouldn't hinder you from going on an exchange.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I don't remember it to be a difficult process. I spend some time looking at possible subjects (you are only allowed to choose between subjects in the "exchange" subject catalog). You then have to apply for a max of 8-10 courses at VU in the beginning. They did not approve all of the classes that I applied for so it ended up taking some time for me to find classes that both VU and KU could approve. The way I understood it, you aren't allowed to take classes that are part of a research master, which limited the psychology courses that I could take. But I managed and both universities were of great help in the process.

 If I had any questions I could write to the "exchange officers", who were very sweet and helpful. They were also very quick at responding to my emails.
VU would send out long e-mails with a lot of information about important deadlines and what to thing about before arriving.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: See comment above

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I wasn't allowed to take some classes, but I got all the classes that I (at the end) chose to take.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
It might seem overwhelming and you'll need some logistical skills to put together your own plan for the semester. But it's more the pre-approval of subjects which can be an annoying process. You can sign up for a maximum of 6 subjects (you usually have 5 in total pr semester) and the different periods (there are 3) have different deadlines for registering. When a period starts you have 1 week to de-register. So in the first period, I signed up for three courses and tried out all three of them in the first week before choosing my final two classes for that period. You can do the same with periods 2 and 3, as long as you only signed up for a total of 6 classes at the same time. 

How it worked was, that VU would add the courses that I had sent to them (and that they had approved) to my plan. Then I could choose which classes to sign-up for.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic level wasn't that different from KU. The number of readings/homework differed from class to class. I found my classes to be very interesting and I personally liked that the types of homework and teaching style differed.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I think I only had master-level courses. Some were of a higher level, but I'm not sure I felt the difference as the courses, in general, were different.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: They were similar. I had lectures, but also some classes with group work, which differed from each other. I also had one class where we did fieldwork on a goat farm, which I really enjoyed. It really depends on what classes you choose to have. Most classes have a good description, some more detailed than others.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Essentials of Media Psychology (instead of an elective)
Sensemaking in Organization (instead of Work and Organizational Psychology)
Changing Organizational Culture (instead of Work and Organizational Psychology)
Disability and Development (instead of an elective)
Advanced Organizational Research Skills (instead of advanced method)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I found all of them very interesting. It was nice to have very different courses.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: 10 euros for membership at the FAM association

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Public transport is similar to at home (so expensive).
Some groceries were (either a bit or a lot) cheaper than in DK, incl. alcohol, soft drinks, coffee, etc.
Activities and dining out were similar in price.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There were a lot of different sports teams/activities that you could join. They also had drama, dance, and other types of creative classes on campus. 
There were different student associations that you could sign up for (some with a small members fee), some of which were connected to a specific faculty or study line.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I signed up to become a member of the FAM association, where everyone is welcome. I paid a members fee of 10 euros for a year. They had a lot of different events throughout the semester and it was a nice way of meeting other internationals as well as Dutch people. If you would like to, the association will assign you a "family" (of 4-6 people) based on your interest. You'll then get a budget lasting a semester that you can spend on activities that you would like to do together as a family. I highly recommend doing this and becoming a member of FAM.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Explore the city of Amsterdam and go to some of the museums as well as the city hall. Visit some of the cities nearby! There are so many pretty cities around Amsterdam (ex. Haarlem, Utrecht, den Haag, etc.). There are also castles and fortresses around Amsterdam. The public transport is good so it's easy to travel around.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
The local culture doesn't differ that much from Danish culture. I just thought that it was funny to experience the differences, but I didn't experience a "cultural shock". 
However, the city (and the country in general) is very international, so there are people from all over the world – only those that are born in the Netherlands can have a nother cultural background.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Sign up for a student association and the buddy program. That was how I got Dutch friends! And attend all different kinds of social events.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
I found the traffic to be more chaotic than in DK. People are not following the "rules" as much so pay extra attention to that! Giving tips is kind of similar to ad home, but I felt like people were doing it more in the Netherlands than in DK.
When arriving, I was told that a lot of Dutch people love their agenda/calender and that they like to plan stuff in advance. I didn't find it to be that extreme (similar to at home), but maybe still a good idea to keep that in mind.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The biking culture. I love to bike so it was great that i could continue to do that! The similarities in culture also made it easier to adapt and plan activities with others. I also liked that it isn't as formal (ex. the relationship between teacher and student) like it is in DK.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Have an open mind and be ready to experience and explore new things!
Almost everyone speaks (at least some) English, but try to learn the most basic phrases in dutch.
You only have to pass your subjects, because the grading systems are different and KU doesn't want to "translate" and transfer the grades. So all your subjects will just be a pass at KU (unless you don't pass a subjects ofc)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Get a bike! Either buy a used one or sign up for Swapfiets. 
Get yourself an OV-card (dutch version of Rejsekort) and if you get a Dutch bank account you can sign up for a subscription that can give you some discount on public transport.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new people from all over the world, as well as experiencing a new culture (as well as learning about other cultures from my friends), and exploring new cities!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I don't know. I didn't think that there were any great challenges during my stay.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
